summary: Jesus tells the temple leaders of two sons, one who refused but went, and of tenants who kill the owner’s son. The leaders see He means them.
key_insight: Twice Jesus asked the leaders to judge a story, and twice they gave the right verdict: the son who went did his father’s will, and wicked tenants deserve to lose the vineyard. Only after they had pronounced the sentence did they see that “He was speaking of them.”
story: Jesus went on speaking to the chief priests and elders. “But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first and said, ‘Son, go, work today in my vineyard.’ ” The son answered, “I will not,” but afterward he regretted it and went. The father said the same to the second son, who answered, “I go, sir,” but did not go. “Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said, “The first.” {Mt}

Jesus said to them, “Assuredly, I say to you that tax collectors and harlots enter the kingdom of God before you.” John had come to them in the way of righteousness; they did not believe him, but tax collectors and harlots did, and even then the leaders did not relent. {Mt}

“Hear another parable,” {Mt} He said, and He told it in the hearing of the people. {Lk} A man planted a vineyard, set a hedge around it, dug a place for the wine vat and built a tower. {Mk} Then he leased it to vinedressers and went into a far country for a long time. {Lk}

At vintage-time he sent a servant to receive some of the fruit. The vinedressers beat him and sent him away empty-handed. They stoned the next one and wounded him in the head. Another they killed, and so with many others, beating some and killing some. {Mk}

Then the owner said, “What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. Probably they will respect him when they see him.” {Lk} But when the vinedressers saw the son, they said among themselves, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance.” So they took him, cast him out of the vineyard and killed him. {Mt}

“Therefore, when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those vinedressers?” They said to Him, “He will destroy those wicked men miserably, and lease his vineyard to other vinedressers who will render to him the fruits in their seasons.” {Mt} Jesus confirmed it: he “will come and destroy those vinedressers and give the vineyard to others.” When the people heard it, they said, “Certainly not!” {Lk}

Jesus looked at them {Lk} and said, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected Has become the chief cornerstone. This was the LORD’s doing, And it is marvelous in our eyes’? Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation bearing the fruits of it.” {Mt}

The chief priests, the scribes and the Pharisees knew He had spoken the parable against them. They wanted to lay hands on Him that very hour, {Lk} but they feared the multitudes, who took Him for a prophet. {Mt} So they left Him and went away. {Mk}
differences: Only Matthew tells the parable of the two sons and Jesus’ words about John, the tax collectors and the harlots.
In Matthew the listeners answer Jesus’ question and pronounce the tenants’ sentence. In Mark and Luke Jesus pronounces it, and in Luke the people respond, “Certainly not!”
Matthew and Luke say the son was thrown out of the vineyard and then killed; Mark says he was killed and thrown out.
Mark and Luke call the son “beloved,” and only Luke has the owner ask, “What shall I do?”
Only Matthew records “the kingdom of God will be taken from you.” Matthew and Luke add the saying about falling on the stone.

fit.question: Who said the owner would destroy the tenants? In Matthew the listeners say it (21:41). In Mark and Luke, Jesus says it, and in Luke the people answer, “Certainly not!” (20:16).

points.label: Question, answer, confirmation
points.text: Jesus asked what the owner would do. Matthew records the answer some listeners gave; Mark and Luke record Jesus repeating that verdict in His own words. A teacher who asks a question and then confirms the answer is speaking with his hearers, not against them.

points.label: Different voices in one crowd
points.text: Luke says Jesus told this parable to the people, with the leaders standing by (20:9, 19). Those who answered at first spoke about the story. Others, catching where it pointed, recoiled: “Certainly not!” McGarvey reads the scene this way.

fit.note: In a crowded court many voices spoke. Each writer records part of a real exchange, and the parts fit together.
fit.short: Listeners gave the verdict, Jesus confirmed it in His own words, and others in the crowd, seeing the point, cried “Certainly not!”

scene.label: Isaiah’s vineyard
scene.text: Jesus’ opening, a vineyard with a hedge, a winepress and a tower, comes almost word for word from Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard. There God says plainly, “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel,” and that He “looked for justice, but behold, oppression” (Isaiah 5:7). Every listener knew whose vineyard this was.

scene.label: Owners far away
scene.text: In Jesus’ day much farmland in Galilee and Judea belonged to owners who lived elsewhere and leased it to tenants for a share of the crop. Quarrels over rent, and even violence against an owner’s agents, were not unknown. The story was easy to picture.

scene.label: The rejected stone
scene.text: Jesus quoted Psalm 118:22–23, from the same psalm the crowds had sung two days earlier: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the LORD!” (118:26). The builders were Israel’s leaders. The stone they threw away would become the cornerstone that holds the building together.

scene.label: A stone that breaks and crushes
scene.text: The saying about falling on the stone recalls Isaiah 8:14–15, where the Lord is “a stone of stumbling” over which many will fall and be broken, and Daniel 2:34–35, where a stone cut out without hands crushes the kingdoms of the world.

witnesses.matthew: Alone records the two sons, and sets three parables in a row aimed at the leaders (21:28–22:14). He alone keeps the hard words “the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation bearing the fruits of it.”
witnesses.mark: Tells of the tenants with the most servants and rising violence, “beating some and killing some,” and calls the son “his beloved,” the word the Father used of Jesus at His baptism (Mark 1:11).
witnesses.luke: Says Jesus told the parable to the people, and records the owner’s question, “What shall I do?”, the crowd’s shocked “Certainly not!” and the detail that Jesus “looked at them” before quoting the psalm.

seeing.reveals: Jesus places Himself in the story as the owner’s beloved son, sent last of all after the prophets. He knows the tenants will kill Him, and He says the rejected stone will become the cornerstone.
seeing.living: The son who said no and then went did his father’s will; the one who said yes and stayed home did not. A polite yes to God means nothing without going. And the father still counted the son who changed his mind. It is not too late to regret a no and go.
seeing.ponder: Have you answered God with an “I go, sir” that has never left the house?

preaching.big_idea: God sent His Son last of all; what we do with Him decides everything.
preaching.watch_for: As Nathan did with David (2 Samuel 12:1–7), Jesus lets the leaders judge the story before they see themselves in it (vv. 31, 41). Only then do they perceive “that He was speaking of them” (v. 45).

title: The Two Sons and the Wicked Tenants
